title: Query Optimisation: Plan Space
lead: A shop asks one question, but the DBMS can execute it in several ways. First prove that the alternatives preserve every required row.
goals: Distinguish the parser, rewriter, and cost-based optimizer
Describe query blocks and the System R approach
Apply logical equivalences and safe simplifications
Change join order while preserving predicates and handling cross products

sections.title: One SQL question can have several correct programs
sections.html:
A shop asks for names of customers who bought a product costing more than 100. SQL states the required result; it does not prescribe whether to filter Products before joining, which table to read first, or which join algorithm to use. The DBMS must turn the question into an executable program. Before choosing the fastest program, establish which programs answer the same question.

Use Customers(id,name), Orders(customer_id,product_id), and Products(id,price). A plan can join everything and then test price>100. Another can first remove cheap products and join the survivors. For an inner join these can return the same rows. Rewriting one into the other changes the plan space: the collection of candidates the optimizer may consider.

The query passes through several different decisions. Parsing and semantic checks establish that the syntax, column names, types, and permissions are legal. A rewriter applies rules that preserve meaning. A cost estimator predicts the work of a physical candidate using catalog statistics. A search procedure decides which candidates to examine. These are separate questions: “is it correct?”, “what might it cost?”, and “which alternatives can we afford to explore?” Historical System R organizes optimization around query blocks and retains useful output orders; later lectures develop costing and searching.

Start with a rewrite that needs no table statistics. WHERE amount>20 AND amount>50 is equivalent to WHERE amount>50: every value above 50 already passes the first test. WHERE 2=3 produces an empty filtered input. Be careful with the operator above it: SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE 2=3 without GROUP BY still returns one row containing 0.

See a query block rather than memorize its name

SELECT C.id FROM Customers AS C
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders AS O
              WHERE O.customer_id=C.id);

The outer SELECT over Customers is one block; the inner SELECT over Orders is another. The inner block refers to the current C.id, so it is correlated. EXISTS asks whether a match exists; two matching orders do not duplicate the customer. For one bound customer, supplied costs 12 for a scan and 3 for an index lookup favor the lookup. If the lookup costs 15 instead, the scan wins. These are illustrative costs for that one block evaluation; the complete plan must account for all customers or a valid transformation that avoids repeated evaluation.

Key takeaway

A correct rewrite must preserve each row’s multiplicity. Under SQL bag semantics, the same values with different numbers of copies constitute different results.

sections.title: Move a filter only after checking the available columns
sections.html:
Let Customers contain (1,An), (2,Binh); Orders contain (1,p1), (1,p2), (2,p2); Products contain (p1,150), (p2,40). Work the shop query by hand. Joining Orders with Products first gives (1,p1,150), (1,p2,40), (2,p2,40). Filtering price>100 leaves (1,p1,150); joining Customers yields An.

Now filter Products first: only (p1,150) remains. Joining that with Orders yields (1,p1,150), then Customers again yields An. The same intermediate survivor explains why moving this predicate is legal: price belongs entirely to Products, and an inner join does not preserve rejected products.

Column removal has a different constraint. Once price has been tested, the Products side needs only id for this query. Orders still needs both customer_id and product_id: one links to Customers, the other to Products. Customers needs id for the join and name for the answer. Dropping Orders.product_id before joining Products makes the later comparison impossible.

InputKeep for later stepsWhy
Customersid, namejoin key and output
Orderscustomer_id, product_idboth joins
Products after price filteridjoin key; price test already done

For deterministic AND predicates, applying one filter then the other preserves their conjunction; reversing those filters also preserves it. Inner joins can change grouping and orientation if every predicate is retained at a node where all its columns are available. A predicate needing S.a cannot run inside a subtree containing only R and T.

SQL keeps duplicate copies unless told otherwise. If the example has two identical (1,p1) orders, An must appear twice. A projection that merely narrows each row preserves those copies; silently adding DISTINCT changes the answer. This distinction matters when translating set-based relational algebra rules into SQL execution.

Can Orders be reduced to customer_id immediately because only customer names are returned?

No. product_id is still needed to decide whether each order bought an expensive product. Remove a column only after its final use, not merely because it is absent from SELECT.

sections.title: A useful shortcut is a candidate, not a proof of speed
sections.html:
Filtering Products early reduced three joined rows to one. This makes early filtering an attractive heuristic: a practical rule for finding promising plans. It is not an equivalence proof by itself, nor a guarantee of lowest cost. An expensive function applied to every product might do more CPU work than applying it only to products reached through a selective join.

Early projection saves row width; early selection saves row count. Neither automatically saves the original heap scan. Reading every product to test price still reads every product page. Lecture 15 follows those costs explicitly.

A second heuristic avoids Cartesian products. In R(a), S(a,b), T(b), join R with S on a and S with T on b. Joining R×T first is legal only if the later S join checks both conditions. It can create many pairs, so search often excludes it. Yet if R and T have only two rows each, their four pairs may be cheap to keep in memory. Excluding that route limits the search; it does not establish that every cross product is slow.

Sometimes a valid inferred predicate creates a new connected route. If R.a=S.b and S.b=T.c, equality transitivity gives R.a=T.c. Adding that condition does not remove any valid joined row. Now R can join T before S without a Cartesian product. Do not infer R.a=T.b from the earlier R(a), S(a,b), T(b) chain: S.a and S.b can differ.

Logical candidates still need physical implementations. An equijoin could use block nested loops, indexed nested loops, sorting and merging, or hashing. Check actual prerequisites: a usable index for probes, enough RAM for a hash build, or order for merging. These choices affect cost while retaining the same logical answer.

Finally, test row preservation before reusing inner-join rules for outer joins. A left join retains unmatched left rows with NULLs. Filtering right.price>100 after that join removes NULL-extended rows; putting that condition only inside the right input can leave those rows in the final result. The two placements answer different questions.

Key takeaway

Inner-join reordering rules do not automatically apply to outer joins. Outer joins also preserve unmatched rows. Moving a join or a filter can remove rows that should have been retained.

sections.title: Exercise: repair a rewrite and check duplicate copies
sections.html:
Use R(a,x)=[(1,r1),(2,r2)], S(a,b)=[(1,9)], T(b,y)=[(9,t9)]. The query requires R.a=S.a AND S.b=T.b. Someone builds S join T correctly, then joins R without checking R.a=S.a. List the wrong result before repairing it.

Work through the rows

S join T produces (1,9,t9). Without the remaining predicate, both R rows pair with it: (1,r1,1,9,t9) and (2,r2,1,9,t9). Only the first satisfies R.a=S.a. Keep that condition at the top join. If S is projected early, keep both a and b: one is needed above and one below.

Now consider a different simplification: SELECT L.* FROM R L JOIN R U ON L.a=U.a. If a is a non-NULL primary key, each left row has exactly one right match in the same relation, so replacing the join with R preserves every row once. If R instead contains (1,A),(1,B), the self-join has four matched pairs and returns each left row twice. R alone contains only two rows. Right columns being absent from SELECT is insufficient to remove the join.

Use two checks for a proposed optimization: can each predicate still be evaluated with the available columns, and does each original row appear the same number of times? Only after those checks is a cost comparison meaningful.

quiz.question: Which columns must projection pushdown retain?
options: Only the columns in the final SELECT list
Output columns and every column still needed by later operators
quiz.explanation: Join keys and filter columns remain necessary even when they are absent from the final SELECT list.
